html:
Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, began in 1922 as a technical school and became the leading college of East Africa. It trained much of the region's first generation of independence leaders.

In 1949 it became the University College of East Africa, linked to the University of London, and took students from Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika and beyond. Among those who studied there were Julius Nyerere of Tanzania, Milton Obote of Uganda and Mwai Kibaki of Kenya.

It was also a centre of writing. In 1962 it hosted a famous conference of African writers, where a young student, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, met Chinua Achebe. The campus magazine Transition, founded in Kampala in 1961, carried the debates of the age.

Makerere became an independent national university in 1970. Under Idi Amin it suffered from violence and lack of money, and many teachers fled. It recovered from the late 1980s and is again one of the largest universities in Africa.
sum: Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, began in 1922 as a technical school and became the leading college of East Africa. It trained much of the region's first generation of independence leaders.
